attrs.title: When a Google Ads audit pays for itself
attrs.lead: The moments when a second opinion is worth the most, and what we usually find behind each one.

items.title: Cost per lead has crept up for months
items.text:
Costs rarely jump overnight. They creep up as competitors raise bids, broad match drifts into loosely related searches and old ads lose their edge. Each change is small, so nobody notices until the monthly report looks very different from a year ago.

In the audit we compare the last 12 months month by month, split by campaign, device, location and search term, so you can see exactly when and where costs started rising, and what each cause is costing you now.

items.title: You’re changing agencies or bringing ads in-house
items.text:
Before a handover is the best time to see what you’re inheriting: how the account is built, which settings were changed, what the tracking really counts and which campaigns are worth keeping. You start the new arrangement with a clean list instead of surprises.

We also check who owns the account, Tag Manager and Analytics, and what access you have, so nothing is lost if you part ways with your current agency. You get a list of what to keep, what to fix and what to switch off on day one.

items.title: Performance Max takes most of the budget
items.text:
Performance Max reports very little by default. It often spends on your own brand name, on Display placements or on a few products, while the results look good on paper. When it takes most of the budget, those hidden problems are most of your spend.

We split Performance Max spend by channel, by search category and by product, and compare the leads or sales it reports with what reaches your CRM or store. You see what it really adds, and what to change so it finds new customers.

items.title: Nobody has looked at search terms in a while
items.text:
Search terms are the searches your ads actually showed for. Left alone for a few months, they fill up with job seekers, free-download searches, students and competitors’ products, and each one costs a click.

We read every search term with spend by hand. Each one is sorted into keep, exclude or add as a keyword, grouped by theme and turned into negative keyword lists you can upload the day you get the report.

items.title: You don’t trust the conversion numbers
items.text:
If Google Ads and your CRM disagree, every decision is built on the wrong numbers, and smart bidding learns from them too. Double counting makes campaigns look better than they are; missing calls make good campaigns look weak.

You get a side-by-side of Google Ads and your CRM or store for the same period, action by action, with the reason for every difference and what to change. It’s the first thing we check, because it changes how every other finding should be read.

items.title: You’re about to increase the budget
items.text:
Spending more in an account that leaks just makes the leaks bigger. Extra budget usually flows into the same broad keywords, the same placements and the same brand searches that already waste money.

The audit shows which campaigns are limited by budget and still profitable, and which are wasting what they already have. Extra spend then goes where it brings more leads, after the leaks are fixed.

attrs.label: How the audit works
attrs.html:
How the audit works

Five working days from access to walkthrough. Read-only access is all we need, and we don’t change anything in your account.

  1. You give us read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Tag Manager. On a short kick-off call we ask about your goals, your margins, what a good lead or sale is worth and what worries you most, so the audit focuses on what matters to you.

    You get: A clear brief for the audit.

    • Read-only access, nothing changed in your account
    • Goals, margins and lead values agreed
    • Your CRM or store numbers for the same period
    • Any history: past agencies, changes, suspensions

  2. A Google Ads specialist goes through all eight areas of the account by hand, using the last 90 days and the last 12 months for trends. Automated tools find settings; a person finds the reasons behind the numbers.

    You get: A full list of findings.

    • All eight areas checked, from tracking to settings
    • Search terms read, not just sampled
    • Change history reviewed for what changed and when
    • Landing pages tested on desktop and phone

  3. Each finding gets a value in money per month, an effort level and a priority. Wasted spend is calculated from your own data, so the fix list is ranked by what each change is worth to you, not by how long it takes us.

    You get: A fix list ranked by value.

    • Wasted spend calculated per issue
    • Effort rated low, medium or high
    • Quick wins marked separately
    • Risks noted, such as changes that reset learning

  4. We write the findings in plain English, with screenshots from your account, a scorecard for each area and the fix list. Anyone on your team, or any agency, can follow it.

    You get: The audit report, yours to keep.

    • A one-page summary and scorecard
    • Screenshots from your own account
    • The ranked fix list as a spreadsheet
    • Ready-to-upload negative keyword lists

  5. A 60-minute call where we walk you through the findings, answer questions and agree what to do first. You can fix things yourself, ask your agency, or have us do it. There’s no obligation.

    You get: A clear plan for the next 30 days.

    • 60 minutes with the specialist who did the audit
    • The top fixes agreed in order
    • Questions answered, including the awkward ones
    • Optional quote if you want us to fix it

What exactly we audit

Eight areas, checked by hand

For each area: why it matters, what we check, what we usually find and what we recommend. Every finding in your report comes with evidence from your own account.

Area 1 of 8

Conversion tracking

If the numbers are wrong, every other decision is too, including what smart bidding learns. Tracking is the first thing we check, because a fix here often changes how every other finding should be read.

What we check

  • Every conversion action, its source and counting setting
  • Primary and secondary goals
  • Google Ads numbers compared with your CRM or store
  • Enhanced conversions and consent mode
  • Calls from ads and from the website
  • Offline conversions and values

What we often find

  • ! Leads counted twice through the Google tag and a GA4 import
  • ! Phone calls not tracked, though they bring a third of leads
  • ! Newsletter sign-ups set as a primary conversion, so bidding chases them
  • ! No enhanced conversions, so fewer conversions are matched

What we recommend

  • Keep one source per conversion and set duplicates to secondary
  • Add call tracking from ads and the website, with a minimum call length
  • Move low-value actions to secondary and give each lead type a value
  • Turn on enhanced conversions and check consent mode

Area 2 of 8

Account and campaign structure

Structure decides how budget is shared and how clearly you can see what works. Too many campaigns split the data so thinly that bidding can’t learn; too few hide weak areas behind strong ones.

What we check

  • Campaign and ad group structure
  • Budget split between campaigns
  • Brand and non-brand kept apart
  • Overlap between campaigns
  • Naming and labels
  • Campaigns that should be paused or merged

What we often find

  • ! Brand and non-brand keywords in one campaign, so brand results hide weak generic terms
  • ! Old seasonal campaigns still live and spending
  • ! Campaigns targeting the same keywords and competing with each other
  • ! Ad groups with 40 or more unrelated keywords

What we recommend

  • Separate brand, generic and competitor campaigns
  • Pause or merge campaigns that overlap or have no clear purpose
  • Group keywords into tight themes with matching ads
  • A naming system so anyone can read the account

Area 3 of 8

Keywords and search terms

Search terms show what people actually typed before clicking. With broad match and close variants, they drift further from your keywords every month. This is where most wasted spend hides.

What we check

  • Match types and broad match use
  • Search terms from the last 90 days, read by hand
  • Negative keyword lists and conflicts
  • Keywords with spend and no conversions
  • Quality Score and its parts
  • Missing high-intent keywords

What we often find

  • ! 412 irrelevant search terms costing $2,140 a month
  • ! Broad match on most keywords, with no negative keyword lists
  • ! Keywords that spend every month and never convert
  • ! High-intent searches with no keyword or ad of their own

What we recommend

  • Negative keyword lists by theme, ready to upload
  • Phrase or exact match for core terms where broad match isn’t earning its keep
  • Pause or rework keywords with spend and no conversions
  • Keywords and ads for the high-intent searches that convert

Area 4 of 8

Performance Max

Performance Max decides where your ads show across Search, Shopping, YouTube, Display, Gmail and Maps, and reports very little by default. We look under the summary at where the money actually goes.

What we check

  • Spend on brand searches
  • Channel split: Search, Shopping, Display, YouTube
  • Asset groups and asset ratings
  • Audience signals
  • Product feed coverage and errors
  • Final URL expansion settings

What we often find

  • ! 38% of spend on people already searching for the brand
  • ! Most assets rated Low, with the same images in every asset group
  • ! Final URL expansion sending people to blog posts and the careers page
  • ! No audience signals, so the campaign learns slowly

What we recommend

  • Brand exclusions, with a separate brand Search campaign
  • New images, videos and headlines for each asset group
  • URL exclusions, or final URL expansion switched off
  • Audience signals from your customer lists and website visitors

Area 5 of 8

Bidding and budgets

The right bid strategy depends on how many conversions you get and how reliable they are. The wrong strategy, or the wrong target, wastes budget quietly or stops campaigns spending at all.

What we check

  • Bid strategy per campaign
  • Targets compared with real results
  • Budgets limited by budget or by rank
  • Learning periods and recent changes
  • Seasonality adjustments
  • Device and schedule performance

What we often find

  • ! A target cost per lead 40% below anything the account has achieved
  • ! The best campaign limited by budget while a weak one has budget left over
  • ! Bid strategies changed every few weeks, so learning never finishes
  • ! No adjustments for seasonal peaks

What we recommend

  • Targets set from real results, then lowered step by step
  • Budget moved from weak campaigns to profitable ones limited by budget
  • One change at a time, with time for bidding to learn
  • Seasonality adjustments for known peaks and sales

Area 6 of 8

Ads and assets

Ads decide who clicks and how much each click costs. Generic ads attract the wrong people and lower your ad rank, so you pay more for fewer good leads.

What we check

  • Responsive search ads and ad strength
  • Headlines that match the searches
  • Sitelinks, callouts, images and other assets
  • Offers, prices and calls to action
  • Disapproved or limited ads
  • Ads for each important keyword theme

What we often find

  • ! The same two generic ads in every ad group
  • ! Headlines that don’t mention what people searched for
  • ! Few sitelinks, callouts or images, so ads look small next to competitors
  • ! Disapproved ads nobody noticed

What we recommend

  • Ads written for each service or theme, using the words people search
  • Clear offers, prices and calls to action in headlines
  • All relevant assets added: sitelinks, callouts, images, calls
  • Disapprovals fixed, with a monthly check for new ones

Area 7 of 8

Landing pages

A good ad on a weak page still loses the lead. We test every page your ads send people to, on a phone and a desktop, the way a customer would.

What we check

  • Message match between ad and page
  • Speed on phone and desktop
  • Forms, buttons and phone numbers
  • Trust signals and proof
  • Pages per campaign or theme
  • Tracking on each page

What we often find

  • ! Every ad sends people to the homepage
  • ! Pages take nearly 6 seconds to load on a phone
  • ! The form and phone number sit below the fold on phones
  • ! No reviews, prices or proof near the call to action

What we recommend

  • A page per campaign or service, matching the ad
  • Speed fixes our web team can make, or a list for your developer
  • Form and phone number above the fold on phones
  • Reviews, guarantees and clear prices next to the form

Area 8 of 8

Settings

Settings hide some of the most expensive mistakes, because nobody looks at them after launch. A single setting can send budget to the wrong country or into mobile games.

What we check

  • Locations: presence or interest
  • Language and network settings
  • Display Network on Search campaigns
  • Ad schedule and time zones
  • Auto-applied recommendations
  • Placement and content exclusions

What we often find

  • ! Search campaigns also showing on the Display Network, in apps and games
  • ! Locations set to “presence or interest”, so ads show outside the service area
  • ! Auto-applied recommendations adding broad keywords without review
  • ! Ads running overnight when nobody answers the phone

What we recommend

  • Display Network off on Search campaigns
  • Locations set to people in, or regularly in, your area
  • Auto-applied recommendations off, reviewed by hand instead
  • An ad schedule that matches when you can take calls

attrs.title: Where Google Ads budgets leak
attrs.lead: The issues we find in most audits. Here is what each one looks like inside the account, and how we fix it.

items.title: Broad match with no negatives
items.problem: Broad match keywords run with no negative keyword lists, so ads show for loosely related and irrelevant searches.
items.fix: Negative keyword lists built from your search terms, and tighter match types where broad match isn’t earning its keep.

items.title: Performance Max buying your brand
items.problem: Performance Max spends on people already searching for your brand name, who would have found you anyway, and reports them as new conversions.
items.fix: Brand exclusions in Performance Max, with a separate low-cost brand campaign.

items.title: Conversions counted twice
items.problem: The Google tag and an imported GA4 goal both count the same lead, so results look twice as good as they are.
items.fix: One conversion source per action, with the duplicate set to secondary.

items.title: Ads in apps and games
items.problem: Search campaigns are opted in to the Display Network, and the budget drains into mobile apps and games.
items.fix: Display Network switched off on Search, and placement exclusions for apps and games.

items.title: Every ad sends people to the homepage
items.problem: Every ad sends people to the homepage, so visitors have to hunt for what they searched for.
items.fix: Landing pages per campaign or theme, with the form or phone number above the fold.

Companies we’ve audited, and what we found

Who they are, why they asked for an audit, what we found and the value it added. Pick a company to read its story.

HarbourlinePhysio

Physiotherapy clinicsAudit, fixes by their own team · 5 days

The company
Three physiotherapy clinics with online booking, spending about $19,000 a month on Google Ads.
Why they asked for an audit
Bookings had flattened while spend kept rising. The owners didn’t know whether to blame the ads, the website or the season.
What we found
  • $2,140 a month on irrelevant searches such as “physio jobs” and “free exercises pdf”
  • 38% of Performance Max spend on their own brand name
  • The booking form counted twice, and phone calls not tracked at all
  • Search campaigns also showing in mobile games
The value it added
Their own team made the top four fixes in a week, straight from our fix list. $4,860 a month moved from waste into the campaigns that brought bookings.

Before the audit vs after the fixes

  • Wasted spend a month

    Before $4,860
    After $620

    87% lower

  • Cost per booking

    Before $58
    After $39

    33% lower

KitebaseSoftware

B2B softwareAudit before an agency handover · 6 days

The company
A project-management app for construction firms, sold on annual plans after a sales-led demo.
Why they asked for an audit
They were moving from an agency to an in-house marketer and wanted to know exactly what they were inheriting.
What we found
  • The Google Ads account was owned by the agency, not by Kitebase
  • Demo requests counted on every visit to the thank-you page
  • Brand and generic keywords in one campaign, hiding a much higher cost per demo on generic terms
  • No offline conversions, so Google optimised for form fills, not sales
The value it added
Account ownership moved to Kitebase before the handover, tracking was rebuilt, and the new marketer started with a ranked fix list instead of guesswork.

Before the audit vs after the fixes

  • Cost per real demo

    Before $212
    After $138

    35% lower

  • Demos counted correctly

    Before 48%
    After 100%

    108% higher

OakridgeRoofing

Home servicesAudit, then fixes by us · 5 weeks

The company
A roofing and gutter company covering one metro area, where most jobs start with a phone call.
Why they asked for an audit
Cost per lead had crept up 60% in a year, and the owner suspected the budget was simply being spent, not managed.
What we found
  • Locations set to “presence or interest”: 18% of clicks came from outside the service area
  • Calls shorter than 10 seconds counted as leads
  • Ads running overnight with nobody answering the phone
  • Every ad sent people to the homepage
The value it added
We fixed the settings and call tracking and built two landing pages. More real calls came in on the same budget.

Before the audit vs after the fixes

  • Cost per real call

    Before $96
    After $61

    36% lower

  • Calls over 60 seconds a month

    Before 74
    After 118

    59% higher

NorthlineOutdoor

Online storeAudit before a budget increase · 7 days

The company
An online store for hiking and camping gear with about 1,800 products and a Shopping-heavy account.
Why they asked for an audit
They planned to double spend for the summer season and wanted to be sure the extra money wouldn’t go to waste.
What we found
  • 64% of products had never had a click in Performance Max
  • Purchase values included tax and shipping, overstating return on ad spend by 22%
  • Brand searches took 31% of Performance Max spend
  • Feed titles missing size, colour and brand
The value it added
Feed and value fixes went in before the season, so the extra budget went to the products and campaigns that could use it.

Before the audit vs after the fixes

  • Real return on ad spend

    Before 2.1x
    After 3.4x

    62% higher

    Before 36%
    After 71%

    97% higher

Law firmAudit only · 5 days

The company
An employment law firm with two offices, taking cases from employees and small employers.
Why they asked for an audit
Leads looked cheap in Google Ads, but the partners said few were real cases. They wanted an outside view before renewing their agency contract.
What we found
  • 42% of spend on searches for free legal advice and job listings
  • Newsletter sign-ups counted as primary conversions
  • The same two ads in every ad group
  • No negative keyword lists at all
The value it added
The firm kept their agency and handed them our fix list. Three months later, far more of the leads were cases worth taking.

Before the audit vs after the fixes

  • Cost per qualified case

    Before $410
    After $265

    35% lower

    After 17

RosterlyScheduling

Subscription softwareAudit, fixes together · 4 weeks

The company
A shift-scheduling app for restaurants and cafés, sold as a monthly subscription after a free trial.
Why they asked for an audit
Free trials were growing but paid sign-ups weren’t, and they couldn’t see which campaigns brought paying customers.
What we found
  • Free trials tracked, but not paid subscriptions
  • Display Network on in Search campaigns: $1,900 a month in apps
  • A bid target 45% below anything achieved, so the best campaign barely spent
  • A competitor campaign with no conversions for five months
The value it added
Paid sign-ups now flow back to Google Ads, the waste is switched off and the budget moved to the campaign that had been held back.

attrs.lead: Can’t find your answer? Ask us on a free 30-minute call.

items.question: What does a Google Ads audit include?
items.answer: Tracking, structure, keywords and search terms, Performance Max, bidding, budgets, ads, assets, landing pages and settings, with wasted spend shown in money and a ranked fix list.

items.question: How much does a Google Ads audit cost?
items.answer: It’s a fixed price, quoted after a short call, based on the size of the account.

items.question: Do you need full access?
items.answer: No. Read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Tag Manager is enough, and we don’t change anything in your account.

items.question: How long does a Google Ads audit take?
items.answer: Five working days from access to the report, then a 60-minute walkthrough call.

items.question: Do I have to hire you to fix it?
items.answer: No. The fix list is written so your team or your current agency can work through it. If you want us to do it, we’ll quote separately.

items.question: How often should I audit my Google Ads account?
items.answer: A full audit once or twice a year, and whenever results change sharply or you change who manages the account.
